newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish KGHM copper combine eager to start sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Polish KGHM copper combine eager to start sell-off.

text.p: Poland's KGHM Polska Miedz SA hopes the Privatisation Ministry finalises this month its agreement with the consortium picked to advise in the copper concern's privatisation, the KGHM spokesman said on Tuesday.

In late June the ministry picked a consortium of Barclays de Zoete Wedd, Union Bank of Switzerland and Wielkopolski Bank Kredytowy SA brokerage to advise it in the sale of KGHM, but has yet to finalise the deal with the three advisers.
"If the agreement is signed this month the advisor can get to work and the whole process of privatisation will finally begin," Piotr Bielawski told Reuters.

Analysts have said that if the privatisation ministry failed to clinch the deal before the ministry is dissolved on September 30, in line with a government reform scheme, the process could be delayed for many more weeks.

From October, all remaining sell-offs will be governed by the Treasury's privatisation agency, but the privatisation ministry's spokesman said the contract with KGHM's advisers would be signed before the hand-over. @
"Documents are being completed and in this month the agreement will be signed," Jerzy Godula told Reuters.

KGHM's Bielawski said that if the advisers now begin work on privatisation of the $2-3 billion firm, KGHM shares could be floated in Warsaw and London around the turn of the second and third quarter of 1997.
"Bourse entry in the second or third quarter (of 1997) is realistic if the adviser begins work right now," he said. @

Under the goverment's tentative plan Poland would reduce its stake in Polska Miedz to 49 percent, up to 15 percent of the remaining 51 percent would be set aside for KGHM employees and about 36 percent would be offered at public offerings.

The ministry had said the adviser would decide the break- down between domestic and international offers, likely to take place on the Warsaw bourse and in London in the form of Global Depositary Receipts (GDR).
Bielawski also said that KGHM was determined to shed some non-core activities, such as a costly transportation system which employs 1,700 out of the company's nearly 40,000 workers.
"In our restructuring programme, many types (of KGHM's) auxiliary services will be transformed into (separate) firms, or the alternative would be laying off employees," he said.

He also said that in 1996 KGHM would not increase wages above the average rate of inflation, running at 20.5 percent in August. He said the average wage in KGHM is just below 2000 zlotys ($720) per month.
In 1995 KGHM produced 405,739 tonnes of electrolytic copper, 964 tonnes of silver and 473 kilorgrammes of gold.
It plans to increase its copper output to 470,000 tonnes per year by 2000, while raising its silver output to 1020 tonnes and gold to 500 kg.
